Loop Conductor: Node ≥ 22, zero runtime dependencies · Claude CLI subprocesses · git worktrees

Loop Conductor: A minimal kernel that takes a one-line brief to a reviewed, tested, locally merged commit. A router agent picks the next action from a closed set; the kernel executes and records it. A human decides twice.
Loop Conductor: Review is only binding if it is bound to a commit hash. That single rule is what the rest of the kernel protects.
Loop Conductor: Code gets reviewed at one commit and merged at another.
Loop Conductor: Approval is bound to the branch head and re-checked at the merge gate.

Loop Conductor: One model call decides, and it decides only which action. The router sees the recorded facts — never the spec, the diff or the code — and returns one of eight action names. Everything with a side effect (spawning an agent, committing, opening a gate, writing state) is plain deterministic Node. A bad run is therefore either a wrong action name, which is one line in a log, or a kernel bug, which is a failing test — never both at once.

Loop Conductor: Node ≥ 22 with zero runtime dependencies. Every agent spawn is a fresh claude -p session with fixed tools; the target repository only ever sees git worktrees and a throwaway merge candidate. state/ and dossier/ on disk are the source of truth, so the run can be killed at any moment and restarted.

Loop Conductor: Open source, solo. 17 tasks run, 10 merged to main, 16/17 one-shot maker pass, $248.67 total API spend — self-reported from Nolan’s own run ledger; the README documents the method. $148.60 of that spend bought zero shipped code, and the current architecture is the response to those failures. Work packages and the plan action are not implemented yet.

Loop Conductor: # Loop Conductor
A minimal kernel that runs an agent loop end to end: a **router agent** picks the next action from a closed set, the kernel executes it, records the facts, and stops at the two gates where a human has to decide — approving the spec, and approving the merge. Everything else — retries, budget, worktrees, the pre-commit regression, branch cleanup — is machine-owned.

## Architecture
Read it top to bottom:

Loop Conductor: - **Operator.** The CLI and the local dashboard are the only ways in. The dashboard holds no state of its own: it rebuilds its view from disk on every request …
- **Kernel.** `npm run conductor -- run` is one plain Node process with no dependencies. Each scheduler step is one *routing round* …
- **Agents.** Every spawn is a fresh `claude -p` session …
- **Disk & git.** `state/` and `dossier/` are the source of truth, so `run` can be killed at any moment and started again …
Live Interpreter: Two-way meeting interpretation that never joins the call and never goes silent.
Live Interpreter: Solo · open source
Live Interpreter: Chrome MV3 offscreen document · Web Audio · WebSocket · Native Messaging · Node host

Live Interpreter: Real-time two-way interpretation for Zoom, Google Meet and Teams. Nothing joins the call: the meeting app only ever sees an audio device, so the other side installs nothing and consents to nothing.
Live Interpreter: The product decision and the security decision are the same shape: put the thing that must not leak — the meeting bot, the API key — outside the surface that is exposed.
Live Interpreter: The audio device disappears mid-stream and the call goes silent.
Live Interpreter: The original path stays open underneath; translation ducks it, never replaces it.

Live Interpreter: Why the original audio is never switched off. Routing the meeting through the translator and playing only the translation is cleaner, and it is wrong: every failure in that chain — a dropped socket, a stalled model, a device that disappears — arrives at the user as silence, and silence is indistinguishable from a quiet room. So the direct path opens at connect time and stays open for the whole session; translation is mixed on top and ducks it while speaking. A total failure of the translation layer degrades to “a meeting you can hear”.

Live Interpreter: Chrome MV3 with an offscreen document (the Service Worker only orchestrates; getUserMedia, AudioContext and the WebSocket live in the offscreen page), Web Audio, Native Messaging to a local Node host, and BlackHole virtual audio devices on macOS. One runtime dependency: a WebSocket library. Long-lived keys stay on the local host; the page uses short-lived credentials.

Live Interpreter: Open source, solo. macOS · Chrome ≥ 116 · Node ≥ 22. Meeting-mute sync covers Google Meet today. 45 automated tests run the whole chain against a mock backend for free; the paid real-link check is one command at about $0.05 a run. The README is in Chinese and the 60-second demo is not recorded yet.

- **下行**：会议 app 输出 → BlackHole 截获 → 翻成你想听的语言 → 你的耳机

chain-pulse: Nightly, zero-dependency Ethereum data pipeline whose heartbeat lives in git.
chain-pulse: Solo · open source · runs nightly
chain-pulse: Node ≥ 22 only · raw JSON-RPC · hand-decoded ERC-20 logs · offline fixture tests

chain-pulse: An unattended pipeline that collects public Ethereum mainnet data and crypto funding signals every night, computes the metrics, writes a Markdown report and commits it — whether or not the run succeeded.

chain-pulse: A pipeline that only commits on success goes quiet exactly when you need to know. The status file is committed on every run, so the heartbeat is visible in git history without a dashboard.
chain-pulse: A public RPC endpoint flakes at 3 a.m. and nobody is watching.
chain-pulse: Multi-endpoint failover with backoff; STATUS.md committed on every run, success or failure.

chain-pulse: Commit the status every run, success or failure. Public RPC endpoints flake, and a pipeline that only commits on success goes quiet exactly when you need to know. chain-pulse writes reports/STATUS.md on every run and commits it even when collection fails, so the heartbeat — and each failure — is visible in git history without a dashboard.

chain-pulse: Node ≥ 22 only, no npm packages. Raw JSON-RPC (eth_blockNumber, eth_feeHistory, eth_getBlockByNumber, eth_getLogs), hand-decoded ERC-20 Transfer logs, multi-endpoint failover with exponential backoff, and unit tests that never touch the network.

chain-pulse: Runs nightly, unattended and read-only: public Ethereum mainnet data plus a funding RSS feed, no keys, no trading endpoints. The daily report lands in reports/latest.md. The README is in Chinese.

chain-pulse: # chain-pulse
夜间自动运行的数据管道：EVM 链上指标 + 加密融资信号，两个业务模块共享同一套无人值守基础设施（调度 / 落盘 / git 心跳 / 告警）。每晚 cron 触发：采集以太坊主网公开数据与融资 RSS → 聚合指标 → 生成 Markdown 日报 → git 固化。
## 设计要点

chain-pulse: - **零依赖**：仅 Node ≥22 内置能力（`fetch`、`node --test`），不装任何 npm 包
- **裸 JSON-RPC**：不经 ethers/web3 封装，直接走协议层（`eth_blockNumber` / `eth_feeHistory` / `eth_getBlockByNumber` / `eth_getLogs`）
- **手工解码 ERC-20 Transfer 事件**：从 `topics` 抽 indexed 地址、从 `data` 抽 uint256 金额
- **多端点故障转移 + 指数退避**：公共 RPC 不稳定是常态，失败换端点重试
- **测试禁网络**：单测全部离线跑纯函数，fixture 驱动
- **只读**：只查公开链上数据，不持有私钥、不接任何交易/下单接口
## 每日产出
`reports/YYYY-MM-DD.md`（另有 `reports/latest.md` 副本）…每次运行（无论成败）都会写 `reports/STATUS.md`
AMM DEX: Uniswap-V2-style AMM from scratch; the pair trusts nothing but its own balances.
AMM DEX: Solo · B.Eng. capstone
AMM DEX: Solidity · Foundry · Next.js — reference architecture: Uniswap V2

AMM DEX: A constant-product automated market maker written from scratch in Solidity — factory, pair and router — with a frontend for swapping and providing liquidity. Awarded outstanding undergraduate capstone.
AMM DEX: The router computes the trade, but the pair re-derives it from its own balances and reverts if the invariant breaks. Correctness lives where the money is.
AMM DEX: A caller hands the pool the wrong numbers for a swap.
AMM DEX: The pair re-derives every amount from its own balances and reverts on the invariant.

AMM DEX: Why the tokens arrive before swap() is called. The caller transfers the input tokens to the pair first, and only then calls swap. It reads backwards — you hand over the money before asking for anything — and it is what lets the pair trust no one: it measures its own balance change instead of believing a parameter, so one invariant check at the end covers every path into the function at once.

AMM DEX: Solidity contracts (factory, pair, router; pair creation, swaps, add / remove liquidity, LP token mint and burn) following the Uniswap V2 architecture, a Foundry test suite for the swap and liquidity paths, and a Next.js frontend against the deployed contracts.

AMM DEX: Student work — a B.Eng. capstone, solo, awarded outstanding undergraduate capstone — and a year older than the rest. It stays because it is where the habit behind the other systems started: the component holding the state validates the state itself, and never trusts a caller’s arithmetic.

Backend or full-stack work on systems where being wrong has a cost — payments and settlement, trading, or the infrastructure underneath an AI product. TypeScript and Node day to day, plus a year of production experience in a team and four systems taken end to end solo. Open to relocation, and to remote.

When Providing Liquidity, the Most Important Variable May Not Be APR — It’s the Range: In the chart:
Blue: LP payoff
Yellow dashed line: holding the risky / Meme asset
Grey dashed line: holding stablecoins
For concentrated-liquidity AMMs such as Uniswap V3, the defining variable of an LP position is often not the APR.
It is the price range.
Suppose ETH is trading at 3,000 USDC.
Providing ETH/USDC liquidity between:
2,800–3,200
and
2,000–5,000
creates two fundamentally different positions.

When Providing Liquidity, the Most Important Variable May Not Be APR — It’s the Range: A narrower range concentrates more capital around the current price and therefore increases capital efficiency.
If ETH keeps trading back and forth between 2,800 and 3,200, your liquidity participates in more swaps and can potentially earn more fees.
But the trade-off is equally clear.

When Providing Liquidity, the Most Important Variable May Not Be APR — It’s the Range: As ETH rises, your ETH is gradually sold into USDC.
As ETH falls, your USDC is gradually converted into ETH.
Above 3,200, the position eventually becomes almost entirely USDC.
Below 2,800, it becomes almost entirely ETH.
And once price moves outside your range, the position stops earning swap fees until price comes back into range or you reposition the liquidity.
That is why I now think the first question about an LP position should not be:
“What APR does this range offer?”

When Providing Liquidity, the Most Important Variable May Not Be APR — It’s the Range: Instead, I ask:
If price reaches the upper bound, am I comfortable effectively selling the asset?
If price reaches the lower bound, am I comfortable converting my stablecoins into that asset?
If the answer to both is yes, the range may actually make sense.
A Narrower Range Is Not Automatically Better
A narrow range simply concentrates more liquidity into a smaller price interval.

When Providing Liquidity, the Most Important Variable May Not Be APR — It’s the Range: That improves capital efficiency, but it also makes the position more sensitive to price movement.
When price stays inside the range and keeps oscillating, LPs can do very well.
But once a strong directional move develops, the position converts into a single asset much faster and can quickly move out of range.
So the goal is not to perfectly predict the exact top and bottom.
The goal is to find a range where:

When Providing Liquidity, the Most Important Variable May Not Be APR — It’s the Range: price has a reasonable probability of spending time, and you are comfortable with the asset conversion that happens at both boundaries.
What About Meme Coins?
The immediate reaction is often:
“Meme coins are too volatile. Impermanent loss is too high. LPing them makes no sense.”
I think that conclusion is too simplistic.
Meme coins are volatile, but they also tend to have extremely high turnover.
And high turnover can generate substantial trading fees.

When Providing Liquidity, the Most Important Variable May Not Be APR — It’s the Range: So Meme LPs can absolutely have value.
The important distinction is that:
the source of your return and the source of your risk are different.
You earn: fees generated by trading volume.
You risk: inventory being transformed by persistent directional price movement.
Imagine a Meme coin trades like this:
1 → 0.8 → 1.1 → 0.9 → 1.05
There is a lot of volatility and turnover, but the final price has not moved very far.

When Providing Liquidity, the Most Important Variable May Not Be APR — It’s the Range: That type of environment can be relatively attractive for an LP.
Traders keep crossing the pool, while the LP keeps collecting fees.
Now compare that with:
1 → 1.5 → 3 → 5 → 10
During the rally, your Meme inventory is continuously sold into stablecoins.
The token may eventually be up 10x, while your LP position has already converted most of the exposure into stablecoins.
The opposite is also true.
If price goes:
1 → 0.5 → 0.2 → 0.05

When Providing Liquidity, the Most Important Variable May Not Be APR — It’s the Range: the LP continuously uses stablecoins to buy the falling token.
Eventually, you can end up holding a large directional position in the Meme coin.
That is why the biggest problem for a Meme LP is not simply “high volatility.”
It is:
high volatility combined with a strong directional trend.
High-turnover sideways markets can be attractive for LPs.
Persistent rallies or persistent declines can turn LPs into the counterparty of trend-following traders.

When Providing Liquidity, the Most Important Variable May Not Be APR — It’s the Range: And even sideways volatility is not guaranteed profit.
Fees still need to compensate for impermanent loss / LVR, gas costs, rebalancing costs and the tail risk of the token itself.
So My LP Evaluation Order Has Changed
I now look at:
Price structure → Range → Trading volume → APR
not:
APR → Deposit capital.
A pool may show 100% APR, but if the token is in a strong one-way rally, I may still avoid it.

When Providing Liquidity, the Most Important Variable May Not Be APR — It’s the Range: Meanwhile, a 30% APR pool with stable volume, persistent range-bound trading and a manageable liquidity range may actually be a much better market-making opportunity.
This is especially true for Meme coins.
I prefer to think of Meme LPs as:
short-duration market-making strategies
rather than:
“depositing tokens and waiting for yield.”
A simple mental model for LPing is:

When Providing Liquidity, the Most Important Variable May Not Be APR — It’s the Range: I am willing to continuously sell into strength and buy into weakness inside this range. The AMM executes the inventory conversion automatically, and I receive trading fees in return.
Once you think about LPs this way, the trade-off becomes much clearer.
Think a Meme coin can go 10x?
Holding the token may be the cleaner trade.
Think it will churn inside a range with heavy turnover?
That is where LPing starts to become interesting.
LP yield is never free.
When Providing Liquidity, the Most Important Variable May Not Be APR — It’s the Range: Trading fees are compensation for taking inventory risk and providing liquidity to the market.

After LLMs Got Stronger, We Deleted Some Nodes from Our Agent Workflow: When we first built Loop, we split the process into many nodes: analysis, decomposition, implementation, Review, and we tried to design the failure branches upfront. That was fine at the time. The models were limited, so the engineering process had to prescribe a path for them. Otherwise, things could easily spin out of control.

After LLMs Got Stronger, We Deleted Some Nodes from Our Agent Workflow: Later, as models got much better at reasoning, tool use, and context understanding, we started to feel that too many nodes were holding them back. Pre-orchestration has one problem: you have to guess upfront how the task will unfold. But software development rarely follows your guesses. An Agent might find a gap in the Spec while implementing, or after Review decide it should add tests first rather than change the code right away.

After LLMs Got Stronger, We Deleted Some Nodes from Our Agent Workflow: If every next step is baked into the flowchart, it has to follow the original path even when it sees a better one.
So Loop gradually became a collaboration among several role-based Agents: Router decides the next step based on the current situation, Spec Agent makes the plan and acceptance criteria clear, Maker implements, and Reviewer checks independently.

After LLMs Got Stronger, We Deleted Some Nodes from Our Agent Workflow: But this isn't about letting Agents run wild. The constraints shifted from “which nodes must it pass through” to “what results must it deliver.” Tests must pass. Review must correspond to the current code version. If the main branch changes, verification must be rerun. Safety boundaries like no pushing still can't be bypassed. These are enforced by the code kernel, not by relying on the Agent to follow them on its own.

After LLMs Got Stronger, We Deleted Some Nodes from Our Agent Workflow: We also replaced some process orchestration with Skill and few-shot. Skill spells out what a role should do, the delivery format, the checks, and what it must not do. Few-shot shows it what good judgment looks like, and what looks reasonable but is actually taking a shortcut. A flowchart can only tell you roughly how things should go; few-shot is more like teaching it how to judge a situation. The stronger the model, the more useful these examples are.

After LLMs Got Stronger, We Deleted Some Nodes from Our Agent Workflow: What people do has changed too. We used to approve the execution process frequently. Now we mainly look at two points: first, confirming the Spec, to make clear what we're actually doing; second, confirming the Merge, to decide whether the result should go into the main branch. How it gets there in between is left to the Agents as much as possible.

After LLMs Got Stronger, We Deleted Some Nodes from Our Agent Workflow: Fixed processes are still useful, of course. Compliance, high-risk external operations, and irreversible actions still need clear steps. But for other constraints, it's worth asking again: is this protecting the system, or is it just compensating for what the previous generation of models couldn't do?
In the future, Agent engineering may be more about this: which boundaries must stay, and which nodes can be removed. Having more nodes isn't necessarily an advantage.
